passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel cognitive training program on working memory in adults aged 25–35. Fifty participants were randomly assigned to either the training group (n = 25) or a control group (n = 25) that received no cognitive training. Working memory was assessed using the N‑back task at baseline and after a 4‑week intervention period. The training group completed 30 minutes of adaptive N‑back exercises daily, while the control group engaged in unrelated reading activities. At baseline, mean N‑back scores were 0.58 ± 0.12 for the training group and 0.60 ± 0.10 for the control group. After 4 weeks, the training group’s mean score increased to 0.72 ± 0.11, whereas the control group’s score changed to 0.61 ± 0.09. The researchers reported a statistically significant improvement in the training group relative to controls (p < 0.01). The study suggests that targeted cognitive training can enhance working memory capacity in young adults.
stem: Which of the following best represents the change in mean N‑back scores for the training group?
explanation: The training group’s mean increased from 0.58 to 0.72, a difference of 0.14. The other options underestimate this change.
trap: Option B incorrectly uses the baseline score of the control group (0.60) instead of the training group’s baseline (0.58).

stem: Which experimental design element best supports the conclusion that the training program caused the observed improvement?

options.A: Random assignment of participants to groups

explanation: Random assignment reduces selection bias and ensures that differences between groups are likely due to the intervention, providing causal inference.
trap: Option D focuses on statistical significance but does not address causal mechanisms.

stem: Calculate the effect size (Cohen’s d) for the training group’s improvement. (Use the post‑intervention SD of 0.11 and baseline SD of 0.12.)
explanation: Correct: A) Pooled SD = sqrt[(0.11² + 0.12²)/2] = 0.115, so d = 0.14/0.115 = 1.22. Why the others are wrong: B) 0.61 results from using a difference of only 0.07. C) 0.92 does not equal 0.14 divided by any SD in the study. D) 1.00 does not equal 0.14 divided by any SD in the study.
trap: Using the wrong difference (0.07 gives about 0.61) or a single SD (0.14/0.12 = 1.17) instead of the pooled SD of 0.115.

stem: Which of the following statements is a common misinterpretation of the study’s findings?

options.A: The training program improves working memory in all adults.
options.C: The control group showed no improvement.
options.D: The study used a randomized controlled design.

explanation: The study only included adults aged 25–35, so generalizing to all adults is unwarranted.
trap: Generalizing from adults aged 25-35 to all adults; the sample does not support that claim.

stem: What is the net (between-group) difference in mean N-back score change, training group minus control group?
explanation: Training change = 0.72 - 0.58 = +0.14; control change = 0.61 - 0.60 = +0.01. Net difference = 0.14 - 0.01 = 0.13.
trap: Using the training group's change alone (0.14) ignores the small practice/test-retest gain seen in controls.
